title: Software Development Proposal Template: From Client Brief to Proposal
excerpt: A software development proposal template helps a freelancer or agency explain the work they recommend, what it includes, and what they need from the client. This guide includes four copyable templates covering client-to-freelancer, client-to-company, freelancer-to-client, and agency-to-client communication, connected through one fictional example.

children.text: At a Glance

>A software development proposal template helps a freelancer or agency explain the work they recommend, what it includes, and what they need from the client. This guide includes four copyable templates covering client-to-freelancer, client-to-company, freelancer-to-client, and agency-to-client communication, connected through one fictional example.

A client might know exactly what is frustrating about their business without knowing what to ask a developer to build. A freelancer or software company then has to turn that description into proposed work, while checking which details are still uncertain.

A software development proposal template provides a structure for that response. Its usefulness depends on the information behind it. A polished document can still describe the wrong project when the client and developer mean different things by “booking system”.

The following process starts with the client's brief, moves through clarification, and ends with a proposal both sides can review. Clients can use it before approaching a freelancer or company. Providers can use it to prepare a response grounded in the client's actual needs.
Client templates:
Client to freelancer
Client to agency or company
Provider templates:
Freelancer to client
Agency to client
Software Project Brief vs Software Development Proposal

A software project brief explains the need from the client's perspective. A software development proposal explains how a provider suggests addressing that need, including the proposed work, responsibilities, and conditions behind the offer.

The distinction applies whether the provider is an independent freelancer or an agency. Both need to understand the problem before they can give a useful response, although their responsibilities and delivery arrangements may differ. A company buying software uses the client templates. A company offering development services uses the provider templates.
Direction
What the document should help explain
Client to freelancer
The problem, expected work, available inputs, and help the client needs
Client to agency or company
The problem, requested services, business constraints, and client-side responsibilities
Freelancer to client
The individual's understanding, proposed contribution, questions, and conditions for delivery
Agency or company to client
The company's understanding, proposed services, accountable roles, and conditions for delivery
A provider can help write or refine the brief. A proposal can also start a discussion rather than represent a fully resolved plan.
Upwork's proposal guidance
includes asking project questions and suggesting a conversation as part of a provider's initial response.
A useful sequence is
initial brief → provider response → clarification → scoped proposal → shared review
. Some projects combine these steps, while others need several rounds of discussion. The document names matter less than making its purpose and unresolved decisions clear.
Software Project Brief Template and Example

Choose the client template that matches the provider you are approaching, then copy it into a document or email. Each version contains the core project information and prompts for that particular working arrangement.
Client to Freelancer Brief Template

Use this version when asking an individual developer to assess your project. Explain the work you want that person to handle, the inputs you can provide, and anything that may require help from someone else.
Section
Details to Complete
Project Overview
Project:
[Name].
Prepared by:
[Client and organization].
Prepared for:
[Freelancer].
Date:
[Date].
Project contact:
[Person and role].
Background and Problem Statement
[Explain the current process, the problem to solve, and the people affected.]
Target Users and Functional Requirements
[Identify the user roles and what each needs the software to do. Describe important workflows in ordinary language.]
Business Objectives and Success Criteria
[Describe the intended improvement and how you would recognize it. Separate known measurements from future targets.]
Project Scope and Exclusions
[Identify the essential first-release work, excluded features, later options, and scope decisions still open.]
Existing Systems and Assets
[List available code, designs, content, data, and integrations, with the people who can explain them.]
Required Services
[Identify the discovery, design, development, testing, deployment, or support help you want the freelancer to assess or provide.]
Client Responsibilities and Third-Party Support
[State what your team or another specialist will supply, who is responsible, and whether those inputs are ready.]
Budget and Timeline
[Provide a range or ceiling if known, the target date and its reason, and any start or availability constraints. Mark undecided items.]
Constraints and Dependencies
[Describe relevant platforms, business rules, access limits, privacy or security needs, and inputs the project depends on.]
Communication and Approvals
[Name who answers questions and approves work. Describe feedback arrangements and any existing team the freelancer would join.]
Open Questions and Next Steps
[List what needs clarification. Ask what discussion, assessment, or proposal the freelancer recommends next and whether preparation is chargeable.]
Client to Agency or Company Brief Template

Use this version when approaching a software company for a proposed service or team arrangement. Describe your project's needs and ask the company to identify its service coverage, coordination, and client-input requirements.
Section
Details to Complete
Project Overview
Project:
[Name].
Prepared by:
[Client and organization].
Prepared for:
[Agency/company].
Date:
[Date].
Project sponsor or decision-maker:
[Person and role].
Background and Problem Statement
[Explain the current process, the difficulty it creates, and who is affected.]
Target Users and Functional Requirements
[Identify the user roles, essential tasks, and important workflows the first version must support.]
Business Objectives and Success Criteria
[Describe the intended result and how you would recognize it. Identify existing evidence separately from targets.]
Project Scope and Exclusions
[List essential work, later options, exclusions, and unresolved scope decisions.]
Existing Systems and Assets
[Identify code, designs, content, data, integrations, and the people responsible for the relevant systems.]
Required Services
[State which discovery, design, development, testing, deployment, and support services you want the company to assess or offer.]
Client Responsibilities
[Identify the information, materials, technical support, decisions, and other work your organization will supply.]
Budget and Timeline
[State budget status, the target date and its reason, and internal or external timing constraints.]
Constraints and Dependencies
[Describe relevant platforms, operating requirements, access restrictions, privacy or security needs, and third-party inputs.]
Delivery Team and Communication
[Ask who would coordinate the work, who handles specialist questions, and which staffing or availability assumptions need confirmation.]
Procurement and Evaluation Criteria
[Describe any vendor-selection process, required response format, evaluation criteria, and internal approvals. Mark not applicable where appropriate.]
Open Questions and Next Steps
[List unknowns and what you want the company to propose next. Ask what any preparation or discovery service includes and whether it has a fee.]
How to Complete the Client Brief

Start with what you know about the current process and the people involved, then use the template to identify gaps. The section names organize your answers, but you can describe the work without technical language.
Follow one task from start to finish:
Explain what triggers it, who acts next, and how people know it is complete. Include an important exception if it changes the process.
Separate constraints from preferences:
Identify what is genuinely fixed, such as a system the business must retain. Mark preferred features, dates, and technical choices as open to discussion where appropriate.
Gather supporting material:
Forms, screenshots, diagrams, or sample data can explain details a feature name leaves unclear. State whether each item shows the current process or an idea for the future.

Leave a clear question where an answer is unknown. Identify who can explain an existing system and arrange access so the provider can assess it. Keep existing measurements separate from targets, and explain the reasons behind budget or deadline constraints.
Upwork's scoping guidance
similarly prompts clients to explain business goals, leadership, required work, and timing. It recognizes that an initial request may lack details that need discussion during the interview.
What Work Do You Need the Developer or Company to Handle?

Use the Required Services and Client Responsibilities fields to explain how you and the provider will divide the work. Agree who handles each necessary task so neither side assumes the other will take care of it.
Provider
What to Clarify
Freelancer
Which work the individual will handle, their availability, and which inputs or specialist contributions the client or another professional supplies.
Agency or company
Which services the company offers, who coordinates delivery, which roles are accountable, and which decisions or inputs remain with the client.

You may need development and testing but already have a designer. State whether the design is complete, who will answer design questions, and who approves revisions. Ask the provider to define its deployment or ongoing support coverage when you want it to handle that work.

Also identify any existing team, vendor-selection process, or internal approval that affects the engagement. The provider's response should explain its actual service coverage and delivery arrangements.
Example: An Equipment-Hire Business

The following equipment-hire business is fictional and will appear throughout this guide. Its initial brief deliberately leaves some decisions open so you can see how a provider's questions help turn an early request into proposed work.
Field
Example answer
Problem
Customers email equipment requests. Staff check availability and reply manually. Customers also send follow-up messages asking what is happening.
Users
Customers requesting equipment and staff reviewing requests.
Desired outcome
Customers can submit a request online and receive a clear response, without depending on an unstructured email exchange.
First-version idea
An equipment request form and a staff view for reviewing requests. The way customers receive status information needs discussion.
Existing systems
Staff use a spreadsheet to check availability. The business has branding and an existing paper request form.
Budget and timing
The client has not confirmed either. The business wants to understand a suitable first version before agreeing on a build budget or date.
Client contact
The operations lead can explain the current process and arrange feedback from staff.
Open questions
Does submitting a request reserve equipment? Should the spreadsheet connect automatically? Are online payments needed? Who creates the interface design?
The client would tell a freelancer which work it expects that person to handle. The client would ask a software company to explain its proposed service coverage and contact arrangements.
How Freelancers and Agencies Clarify a Client Brief

Clarification should focus first on questions whose answers could change the work. A provider does not need to settle every screen detail immediately, but it should identify assumptions that affect the proposed outcome, responsibilities, or estimate.

The equipment-hire client's phrase “submit a request” could mean asking staff to check availability or making an immediate reservation. Those are different workflows. A useful response makes the distinction visible before presenting a detailed solution.
The next questions might be:
Does the customer reserve equipment immediately, or must staff approve the request?
Will staff keep checking the spreadsheet manually, or should the software connect to it?
How should customers receive confirmation and the staff's decision?
Does the first version collect payments?
What design work exists, and who will supply or create what is missing?
Freelancer to Client: Clarify Scope, Capacity, and Missing Inputs

A freelancer's initial response should show how they understand the request and identify the answers needed to assess their contribution. It should also explain where the proposed work depends on the client or another professional.
An illustrative response to the fictional brief could be:

“I understand that you need a customer request form and a way for staff to review requests. Does submitting a request reserve equipment, or do staff need to approve it first? Should availability checks remain manual? I would also need to agree who supplies the interface design and customer-facing text.”

The freelancer can then explain the work they are considering taking on and any capacity or specialist limits. This response starts a useful conversation without pretending that the client's initial description answers every delivery question.
Agency to Client: Clarify Service Coverage and Accountability

An agency uses the client's brief to assess project fit, clarify the required services, and check team availability. Its response should identify the client's priorities and explain who coordinates delivery, specialist questions, and client reviews.
An agency could respond to the same fictional project:

“We understand the goal is to move equipment requests into a consistent process. Please confirm how staff approve requests, whether inventory stays manual, and how customers should receive updates. We can then explain which design, development, and testing services our proposal covers, who coordinates the work, and which inputs we need from your team.”
A client can begin with a short enquiry and the information already available.
thoughtbot's published agency process

starts with contact through a project form, phone, or email, followed by discussions about fit, product vision, and intended outcomes before estimating the engagement. The agency can then identify what needs clarification before proposing the work.

The fictional client clarifies that staff must approve requests and check availability manually. The first version will exclude online payments and customer accounts. The application should email customers after they submit a request and after staff approve or decline it. The provider must still identify who will handle design in the proposal.
Software Development Proposal Template

Use this software development proposal template after gathering enough information to describe the work you are offering. Identify unresolved details and explain what you need to decide or investigate before you finalize the offer.
The two versions below are complete copyable formats for different provider arrangements. Choose the appropriate one and replace every placeholder with information about the actual project and offer.
Freelancer to Client Proposal Template

Use this version to explain the work you propose to deliver as an individual. State your contribution and availability, what the client supplies, and any specialist support or unresolved decisions the offer depends on.
Section
Details to Complete
Project Information
Prepared for:
[Client and contact].
Prepared by:
[Freelancer].
Project:
[Name].
Date/version:
[Details].
Reference:
[Brief version or discussion].
Executive Summary
[Summarize the client's problem, intended users, desired outcome, and your recommended contribution.]
Proposed Solution
[Explain how you suggest addressing the problem and why the approach fits the client's needs.]
Scope of Work and Deliverables
[List the work and outputs you will provide, including relevant user roles, workflows, and supported environments.]
Exclusions and Optional Services
[State what is outside this offer. Identify optional services and later work separately.]
Roles, Responsibilities, and Availability
[Describe what you will personally handle, your proposed availability, and any specialist involvement that needs agreement.]
Client Responsibilities
[Identify the designs, content, data, access, decisions, and approvals the client must supply, with a responsible contact.]
Project Timeline and Milestones
[Describe the stages, reviewable outputs, client review points, proposed dates or scheduling conditions, and decisions needed to proceed.]
Fees and Payment Terms
[State the pricing model, amounts or estimate status, payment schedule, and separately charged services.]
Assumptions and Dependencies
[State the conditions, client inputs, external services, and access arrangements your approach and estimate rely on.]
Open Questions
[Identify unresolved requirements and any investigation you need to complete before finalizing the proposal.]
Testing and Acceptance Criteria
[Describe the testing you will perform, the results the client will review, and who will handle feedback or issues and how.]
Deployment, Handover, and Support
[Identify release and handover responsibilities, the support included, and any ongoing services offered separately.]
Relevant Experience
[Provide a concise example of your actual contribution or expertise, with evidence where available.]
Change Management
[Explain how changed requirements will be assessed and discussed for their effect on scope, timing, and cost.]
Next Steps
[State the decision or discussion requested from the client and identify any engagement documents still needed.]
Agency to Client Proposal Template

Use this version to explain how your company proposes to address the client's brief. Identify the included services, delivery arrangement, accountable roles, and conditions behind the estimate so the client can assess the offer.
Wiredcraft's proposal process

gathers client materials such as requirements, wireframes, and briefs before preparing an estimate and proposal. Its proposal also explains the company, team, strategy, and relevant portfolio. Use the Relevant Experience field below to explain your company's actual contribution to comparable work.
Section
Details to Complete
Project Information
Prepared for:
[Client organization and contact].
Prepared by:
[Agency/company].
Project:
[Name].
Date/version:
[Details].
Reference:
[Brief version or discussion].
Executive Summary
[Summarize the client's problem, priorities, desired outcome, and the services your company recommends.]
Proposed Solution
[Describe the recommended solution and delivery approach in terms the client can assess.]
Scope of Work and Deliverables
[Identify included discovery, design, development, testing, deployment, and support services, with the outputs and boundaries of each.]
Exclusions and Optional Services
[State which features or services you exclude and which you offer as separate options.]
Delivery Team and Responsibilities
[Identify the delivery contact and accountable roles. State which team assignments, external contributors, or staffing details need confirmation.]
Client Responsibilities
[List the materials, access, decisions, reviewers, and approvals required from the client.]
Project Timeline and Milestones
[Describe delivery stages, reviewable outputs, proposed dates or scheduling conditions, and client review points.]
Communication and Reporting
[Describe coordination, progress updates, review meetings, and how questions reach the responsible people.]
Fees and Payment Terms
[State the pricing model, amounts or estimate status, payment schedule, and separately charged services.]
Assumptions and Dependencies
[Identify client and third-party inputs, availability assumptions, access requirements, and other conditions behind the proposal.]
Open Questions
[Identify unresolved requirements and any investigation needed before firm delivery commitments.]
Testing and Acceptance Criteria
[Describe included testing, client acceptance checks, and who will handle feedback and issues and how.]
Deployment, Handover, and Support
[Explain release and handover responsibilities, support coverage, and any ongoing service options.]
Relevant Experience
[Provide an accurate, relevant example of the company's contribution, supported by verified results where available.]
Change Management
[Explain how changed requirements are assessed, communicated, and agreed for their effect on scope, timing, and cost.]
Next Steps
[State the proposed discussion, approval, or engagement step and identify any documents still needed.]

A fixed-price offer needs different explanations from an engagement that charges for time worked. State the included work and pricing conditions when offering a fixed price. Explain your rates, estimate assumptions, and how you and the client will review progress and spending when charging for time worked. Describe the model you actually offer.

Write delivery commitments separately from business ambitions. “Provide a staff request-review screen” is proposed work. “Eliminate customer follow-up emails” is a desired business outcome that also depends on customer behavior and how the service operates.

Show optional design or support services separately. Describe their coverage clearly when you include them in the offer. A client should not have to infer the difference from a single total or a list of job titles.
Software Development Proposal Example: Responding to the Client Brief

This fictional example continues the equipment-hire discussion. It illustrates a proposed scope after clarification, rather than a priced offer or a complete specification. The freelancer and agency versions share the intended workflow but describe their responsibilities differently.
Proposed work:

Create a customer request form and a staff review area. Customers receive an acknowledgement after submission and an email when staff approve or decline a request. Staff continue checking equipment availability using their existing spreadsheet.
Included workflow:

A customer submits the required request information. Authorized staff review it, check availability outside the application, and record their decision. Customer-facing text explains that submitting the form does not guarantee a reservation.
Excluded from this version:

Automatic inventory synchronization, automatic reservation allocation, online payment collection, and customer accounts. The provider variations below identify who handles interface design and release.
A proposal should show how the client's answers shape the work. The table below connects the fictional equipment-hire client's answers to proposal content and practical checks the client can review.
Client's Answer
What the Proposal Should State
What the Client Can Review
Staff must approve requests
Scope of Work and Deliverables:
Provide a customer request form and a staff area for reviewing, approving, or declining requests. Explain that submission does not guarantee a reservation.
Submit a sample request and have a staff member approve or decline it. Check that the workflow reflects that decision.
Staff will check availability manually
Scope and Exclusions:
Staff will continue checking the spreadsheet. Exclude automatic inventory synchronization and reservation allocation.
Confirm that the proposed workflow supports staff decisions without promising an automatic availability check.
Customers need email updates
Deliverables and Responsibilities:
Include a submission acknowledgement and an approval or decline email. Identify who supplies the message text and arranges the email service.
Follow a sample request through submission and a staff decision, then check the expected customer emails.
The first version will exclude payments
Exclusions:
Keep online payment collection outside the proposed work.
Check that the scope and estimate do not imply that the provider will build a payment workflow.
Design responsibility remains undecided
Roles, Responsibilities, and Dependencies:
Agree who creates and approves the interface design. State which design inputs the provider needs before starting the related development work.
Check that the proposal assigns design responsibility and explains any effect on the estimate or start conditions.

The freelancer's proposal could place interface design with the client. The agency's proposal could include design among its services. These are two fictional offers. Either type of provider may include or exclude design, so the client should check the actual service coverage.

The proposal should also identify unresolved questions about staff access and the email service. The provider and client need to settle those details before relying on commitments that depend on them.
Freelancer Proposal: State the Individual's Contribution

The freelancer in this fictional example proposes development and technical testing. The client will arrange and approve the interface design. The proposal should explain that dependency so neither side assumes the freelancer will supply design work.
The responsibility statement could read:

“I propose to implement the request form, staff review area, and agreed email notifications. You will provide the approved interface design, equipment information, and message text, with your operations lead reviewing the workflows. I will confirm the release arrangements and estimate after reviewing those materials and the required access.”

The proposal should also explain how staff access their review area, which information the form collects, and who arranges the email service. Those decisions remain open in this example and need resolution before the provider presents a firm build commitment.
Agency Proposal: State the Company's Service Coverage

The agency in this alternative fictional example proposes interface design, development, and testing. Both providers address the same customer task, but their service coverage differs. The client needs to account for those differences when comparing offers.
Its responsibility statement could read:

“Our proposed services include interface design, development, and technical testing for the request-and-review workflow. A delivery contact will coordinate questions and reviews. Your operations lead will supply equipment information and message content, clarify business rules, and approve the design. We will identify the responsibilities and conditions for release in the completed proposal.”

The agency still needs to explain the unresolved access and email-service arrangements. Providing several services does not make those dependencies disappear. It should name or identify accountable roles in its actual offer and explain any staffing assumptions that affect availability.

Either provider can describe a reviewable check: submit a sample request, have an authorized staff member approve or decline it, and verify the expected customer emails. The provider and client must also define edge cases, access rules, and message failures before completing the acceptance checks.
How Clients Compare and Review Software Development Proposals

Compare what each offer includes before comparing its total. Two providers can understand the same business goal and still propose different services, assumptions, or delivery arrangements, so a lower number alone does not explain which offer fits.
Use the brief alongside each proposal and work through the questions below. Ask the provider to resolve differences in writing so the current document reflects what both sides have discussed.
Review area
What to check
Intended result
Does the proposed workflow address the problem described in the brief?
Included work
Are design, development, testing, release, and support included, excluded, or separately offered?
Boundaries
Are related features and later ideas clearly separated from this offer?
Responsibilities
Who supplies materials, answers questions, approves work, and handles external services?
Estimate basis
What does the price or effort estimate cover, and which conditions could change it?
Schedule
What must happen before work starts, and which client or external inputs affect delivery?
Review
What can the client examine or try, who responds to feedback, and how are unresolved issues handled?
Next step
Is the immediate decision a further investigation, a defined stage, or a proposed build engagement?

The fictional freelancer expects the client to arrange design, while the agency includes it in its offer. The client should account for that difference before comparing the offers. Neither arrangement is automatically preferable without considering the client's resources and needs.

Record a later request for automatic stock allocation as a new decision and ask the provider what it changes. Updating the brief and proposed work together helps avoid one document describing manual checks while another implies an automated reservation system.

Keep important commercial and engagement terms explicit too. Identify which documents will address payment, ownership, access, support, and other agreed terms rather than assuming that a brief or generic template settles them.
Final Thoughts

A useful brief gives a provider enough context to ask informed questions. A useful proposal shows what the provider recommends after considering those answers, including the work, responsibilities, and decisions still needed.

Clients can begin with the brief template and mark what they do not know. Freelancers and agencies can then use the proposal template to respond to that specific situation. The next step is to review the two documents together and resolve differences before making commitments that depend on them.
Frequently Asked Questions

These questions address situations that can make it difficult to begin or adapt the process. Use the answers alongside the templates, particularly when you need help defining the work or understanding what preparation a provider offers.
What If I Do Not Know How to Write a Brief for My Project?

Send a short description of what happens today, what is difficult, and what you want to improve. Ask the developer or company what information it needs and whether it can help turn your description into a brief.

You could write: “Customers email us equipment requests, and staff reply after checking availability. I want to move the request process online, but I am unsure what the first version should include. Can you help clarify it and explain your process?” You can begin this conversation without choosing a programming language or writing a technical specification.
Is Help Preparing a Brief or Conducting Discovery Free or Paid?

Ask the provider what its preparation service includes and whether there is a charge before agreeing to it. Distinguish an introductory conversation from work such as investigating existing software, mapping workflows, or testing an integration.

Ask the provider what decisions its proposed discovery service will help you make and what you will receive. That makes the next step understandable without assuming every enquiry requires the same process or fee.
Do I Need a Formal RFP Before Contacting a Developer or Agency?

Check your organization's purchasing requirements first. Follow your organization's request for proposal, or RFP, process when required, and make clear what suppliers must respond to. An initial project enquiry does not have to imitate a formal procurement document simply because software is involved.

Use the client brief to organize the first conversation when your organization has no prescribed process. Give each provider the same current information and relevant clarifications when inviting several providers to respond.
Can I Use These Templates to Improve an Existing Application?

Yes. Add the current application's purpose, the part that needs to change, and the constraints around assessing it. Explain whether the provider can review the code, designs, integrations, and relevant documentation before proposing the work.

Describe migration or continuity needs where they matter. A request to improve one workflow should also identify behavior that must keep working, particularly when people already depend on the application.
What Should I Do If an Important Requirement Is Still Unknown?

Name the unresolved question, who can help answer it, and which proposed work depends on the answer. A small preference may be settled during design, while an uncertain integration or business rule may need investigation before a useful estimate is possible.
Ask the provider to explain that investigation and its effect on the next commitment. Avoid turning an untested assumption into an agreed fact just to make the proposal look finished.
